extracted.intended_audience: general readers and historians interested in Cornish smuggling and maritime social history
extracted.subtask_description: A chapter-length historical narrative and biographical sketches about seafaring smugglers, their social context, reputations, and local practices in Cornwall from the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seafaring qualities of smugglers
rubrics_metrics.description: Contemporaries and historians praise smugglers for their seamanship, audacity, local knowledge, and conduct in emergencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Captain Brenton: “These men... are as remarkable for their skill in seamanship as for their audacity in the hour of danger; their local knowledge has been highly advantageous to the Navy... They are hardy, sober, and faithful to each other... and, when shipwreck occurs, have been known to perform deeds not exceeded in any country in the world.” Examples and anecdotes (shipwreck rescues, piloting dangerous missions) are offered as evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic-benefit justification for smuggling
rubrics_metrics.description: Smugglers were commonly viewed locally as benefactors because they supplied cheaper and (often) better-quality goods than duty-paid trade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: duty-paid goods were largely adulterated, so buying smuggled goods was pragmatically rational. Adam Smith’s observation: refusal to buy smuggled goods would be seen as hypocrisy — the popular view favoured taking advantage of cheaper, superior articles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adam Smith’s moral-economical perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: Adam Smith’s balanced judgment on smugglers: blameworthy for violating the law, but often not for violating natural justice; many smugglers would have been good citizens but for the laws that criminalized their trade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted assessment: smuggler is ‘no doubt blamable for violating the laws of his country, is frequently incapable of violating those of natural justice, and would have been in every respect an excellent citizen had not the laws of his country made that a crime which nature never meant to be so.’ Use this to contextualize popular sympathy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clerical condemnation and catalogue of harms
rubrics_metrics.description: Some clergy (e.g., Rev. Robert Hardy) condemned smuggling as sinful and socially harmful, listing consequences such as informations, fines, seizures, imprisonments and moral injury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hardy’s pamphlet frames smuggling as carrying ‘so many evils, and mischiefs, and sorrows,’ hoping these penalties would discourage participation. Use as an example of moral/reformist arguments against smuggling and their limited practical effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typology of participants in smuggling
rubrics_metrics.description: Smuggling involves three classes: (1) those who employ capital in the trade, (2) those who do the work, (3) those who deal in smuggled articles as sellers or buyers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hardy’s classification emphasises differing moral responsibility and that the ‘moral injuries’ fall principally on the second class (the workers). This typology can be used to parse culpability and social effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Popular complicity and social acceptance
rubrics_metrics.description: Widespread local acceptance and complicity: few voices opposed smuggling; clergy often tacitly benefited; parish officials (clerks, wardens) could silence opposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anecdotes (parish clerks, the question ‘who is there that has not had a tub?’) illustrate why moral exhortations had limited effect. Use these to explain persistence of smuggling despite legal penalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local geography and social infrastructure enabling smuggling
rubrics_metrics.description: Secluded coves, lonely churchyards, secret cellars, poor roads, and the close-knit amphibious character of local populations facilitated smuggling operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Talland churchyard used to store kegs; Hicks’ Court ‘secret’ cellar in St. Ives; narrow bridle-paths and lack of roads around Prussia Cove. These operational features show how physical and social landscapes supported the trade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memorial sentiment and portrayals of dead smugglers
rubrics_metrics.description: Local epitaphs and memorials to smugglers show a range of sentiment—from mild and forgiving to bitter and reproachful—reflecting community attitudes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: Robert Mark’s pious, forgiving epitaph and the more academic/neutral epitaph for Thomas James. Use the style of epitaphs as cultural evidence of popular memory and attitudes toward smugglers and the revenue service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individual character complexities (patriotism vs. criminality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Biographies show smugglers could be resourceful, patriotic in certain contexts (e.g., Johnson refusing Napoleon), and capable of public service despite criminal careers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anecdotes about Tom Johnson’s offers to pilot national expeditions, his refusals to betray country, pardons for service, and later roles (command of a revenue cruiser) illustrate blurred moral/official lines between outlawry and national utility.
